speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I gave Madam Speaker notice of a question of privilege involving the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
At 2.15 p.m. today Madam Speaker tabled before the House of Commons the report of the Auditor General to the House of Commons for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1979, in which there are references to the operation of government. Earlier in the day, before this report was tabled in the House of Commons, there was delivered to the office of each member of Parliament a statement entitled: "Unemployment Insurance: Undetected overpayments in 1978 projected by the Auditor General of Canada, Statement by the Honourable Lloyd Axworthy, Minister of Employment and Immigration, April 16, 1980."

I do not know whether the minister attended or not. Perhaps he did not have any reason to attend. There is no doubt that he was not referring to anything else but the report of the Auditor General as tabled, because in the document which he delivered to all our offices in advance there was the following paragraph:
The Auditor General's annual report, tabled today-
That is in the past tense, "tabled today". It continues:
-estimates that Ul overpayments in 1978 may have amounted to $290 million.
It goes on to quote a number of statistics out of the Auditor General's report.
The fact of the matter is that members of the House of Commons who saw that report were subject to quite an appropriate condition of confidentiality until that matter was tabled here in the House of Commons. I think it is a matter that is quite serious. It involves two things. The minister's behaviour is a discourtesy to the Auditor General in the first place.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: I do not know whether it has escaped his attention or not, but the Auditor General is a servant of Parliament, not a servant of the minister. That is the first thing. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege at the earliest possible opportunity upon being apprised of a set of circumstances which affects the rights and privileges of all members of the House of Commons, their rights and prerogatives in terms of the dissemination of the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House of Commons. Specifically I refer to the fact that in the city of Saskatoon the provincial government, through its Crown corporation, Sask Tel or Saskatchewan Telecommunications, has in fact taken the step of jamming the transmission of the proceedings of this House of Commons to the citizens of Saskatoon.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-JAMMING OF BROADCASTS OF HOUSE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-JAMMING OF BROADCASTS OF HOUSE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
In terms of the responsibility which Madam Speaker has to articulate, and in fact to investigate and take steps with respect to protecting the rights of members of the House of Commons, compels me to raise this matter at this particular point in time. Apparently what has happened is that there has been the transmission, through the facilities under Madam Speaker's chairmanship, of the proceedings of this House to Saskatchewan which has been received by the
equipment of Saskatoon Telecable Limited. This equipment has received the signals and the intention has been that it be carried over the lines owned and controlled by Sask Tel in Saskatoon. What has happened has been an interference with that particular dissemination.
1 would be interested in hearing from the minister responsible, the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), as to what attitude the government takes with respect to this interference and with respect to responsibility for and jurisdiction over broadcasting in Canada, particularly as it relates to the House of Commons. I bring this matter to Madam Speaker's attention as a question of privilege and as a matter which is under her responsibility in terms of the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House of Commons. There has been an interference in the dissemination of the proceedings here to the people of Canada. I ask for a ruling with respect to that matter so that there will be no further interference with the broadcasting to Saskatoon.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I interrupted my speech last night, I was saying that the PQ government was not reliable, that it had abused in the past and would still try to abuse in the future the faith of well-intentioned people. Knowing that a large number of Canadians want a new Canadian constitution, the Parti Quebecois is trying with its referendum in Quebec to get a mandate to negotiate a new agreement with the rest of Canada. We must not be taken in by that PQ stratagem. The new agreement wanted by a great majority of Canadians is an agreement between Canadians in Quebec and in the other provinces within Canada, not an agreement between Quebec on the one side and Canada on the other, not an agreement between two sovereign entities, apart, face to face, as Rene Levesque wants.
So those who would want to give Mr. Levesque a mandate to negotiate a new agreement within Canada are kidding themselves because they should know and remind themselves that the known option, the avowed objective of the Parti Quebecois, is to get out of the federal regime. So sovereignty is their objective, and association is a convenient ploy added by the Parti Quebecois to try and get more votes in the referendum. In 1976, by voting for the Parti Quebecois, the hand went into the wringer, and in 1980, by voting Yes in the referendum the whole arm is going to go through it, and normally when the arm is in the wringer, it is then very difficult to keep the whole body from following.
That is why, through you, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to ask my voters in the riding of Montreal-Papineau and all my fellow citizens in Quebec: Frankly, are you tried of being well in Canada? Frankly, are you tired of belonging to one of the greatest countries in the world? Are you tired of enjoying one of highest standards of living? Are you tired of benefiting from all the advantages and the wealth of the Canadian federation? Do you really have grievances so serious that you think you cannot solve them within Canada? Sincerely, 1 do not believe so. I believe you do not have any reason to be tired of all that and, consequently, it is very important that you vote No on May 20.
The PQ supporters would like us to believe that if the taxes paid to Ottawa by Quebeckers went instead to the Quebec government, this last government could finance the same social programs, provide the same services to the people and generate the same economic advantages. This is false, completely false. There would not be enough money for this, unless of course the taxes of Quebeckers were increased substantially.
During the referendum debate in the National Assembly, the separatists really laid it on. They really showed that ridicule has never killed anyone. The outrageous remarks of
The Address-Mr. Ouellet
agriculture minister Jean Garon were equalled only by his own circumference. How can Mr. Garon seriously pretend that the farmers as a group will be those who benefit most from Quebec sovereignty when neither he himself nor his leader, Mr. Levesque, are willing to guarantee to milk producers the same level of quotas that they now have within the Canadian system? It is all very well to say that the Quebec government will provide farmers with the same subsidies as does the federal government, but if the quotas are reduced, each farmer will lose thousands of dollars because his production will no longer be sold in the other Canadian provinces and because his overproduction will no longer be eligible for the subsidy.
The total contribution of Agriculture Canada to the economic activity of the various Quebec regions represents between $450 million and $500 million annually, without mentioning the assistance given by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which also spends several million dollars a year to promote the agricultural development of certain areas in Quebec. Mr. Garon said nothing about the services which Agriculture Canada provides Quebec farmers through its institutions in Sainte-Foy, its experimental farms in La Pocatiere and Normandin, its Lennoxville research station, and its facilities in Saint-Jean and Saint-Hyacinthe. Mr. Garon also omitted to speak about the considerable assistance given by Ottawa to the Granby farm co-operative, the largest in Canada, and to several other dairy co-operatives in Quebec. In fact, Mr. Speaker, 1 could say that the good farmer who has both feet firmly planted on the ground will be the last to be conned by the separatists.
Since I represent a constituency in the Montreal area, I would also like to tell to Quebec minister Bernard Landry, who brags about doing much for the economic revival in Montreal with his OSE program, that he can brag and boast and pat himself on the back, that he can multiply his television advertisements concerning this program, but he will still look like a school boy watering his rink with his little garden hose while the Canadian government is much better equipped with a big fire hose to do something effective and much more meaningful in the Montreal area. We only have to recall that the Canadian government spends directly each year in the Montreal area about $5 billion in wages, social assistance, subsidies, capital expenditures, guaranteed loans and contracts.
The Canadian government is very much present in Montreal in every sphere. I am thinking of Air Canada, the Canadian National, the National Harbours Board, the major postal installations, Transport Canada with its airport at Mirabel and Dorval, the Federal Development Bank, the National Film Board, Canadair, CBC. If Quebec were to separate, all these companies, all these departments, would leave Montreal or would at least reduce their activities by one-half. To make up for those losses, Mr. Landry would need much more than his small OSE program. The contracts awarded by Ottawa to Montreal-based companies or departments-and I shall con-

Mr. Speaker, I want to remain in this country and contribute to its renewal.

speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, it is certainly with pleasure that 1 have this opportunity of doing my first pleasant duty in this Thirty-second Parliament in extending to Madam Speaker my sincere best wishes on her onerous and demanding task as moderator of this assembly. May Divine Providence guide her in her deliberations. I have every confidence that Madam Speaker's ability, experience and charm will combine to serve this body well. She can be assured of my respect and co-operation at all times.
It is my sincere hope that this Thirty-second Parliament will be a working Parliament, a responsible Parliament, a Parliament ready to address itself to the root problems which plague this great nation of ours. These problems will not be resolved by cosmetic legislation, by the application of a band-aid here or a lollipop there. They will be resolved only if we identify them, gear in on them and put long-term measures in place to correct them. That is why 1 was pleased to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say through the Speech from the Throne that recognition would be given to members of Parliament so that they would have the privilege and the opportunity of stating the cause and the case of the people whom they represent.
I want to read that portion of the throne speech to which I refer. It appears at page 6 of Hansard for April 14, 1980, as follows:
Like all of your colleagues in the House of Commons, you who represent the people of Saskatchewan. Alberta and British Columbia, have a responsibility to represent your constituents to the nation. You also have an extra responsibility in the present circumstances to represent the nation to your constituents. It is a task no one else can fulfil. My government is prepared to co-operate fully in helping you to achieve this.
That is a challenge the Prime Minister has given to us and one which as a representative of the province of Alberta I am prepared to accept; but we do have to have the co-operation of members of the government and they must listen to us in order for us to accomplish this task. This is of fundamental importance. I must stress most emphatically that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) pay special attention to what we have to say because, after all, we are here not only as representatives of Canada, but also as representatives of our respective constituencies and the resources of the province of Alberta, as I interpret this privilege, should exist for all members. We must work together as a Parliament casting partisan gain aside so that the national interest is served. The nation looks to this institution. Parliament, for
leadership, for direction, for the social and political sustenance which will feed the search for identity and the quest for national unity.
The Speech from the Throne refers to the siren call. 1 hear siren calls across Canada; strident, harsh, frightening. Those siren calls would have this nation divided. Those siren calls pit region against region and province against province. They contribute to a further balkanization of Canada. The time for action is now. It is not too late for men and women of good will to address themselves to this fact of life. Now is the time to begin afresh to right wrongs, redress imbalances and bring unity where there is division.
1 represent a riding in Alberta, as I said earlier, but I am first and foremost a Canadian and a Canadian I want to remain, a Canadian from Alberta who is a member of a great confederation, a confederation we must make stronger. Certainly any callousness, especially from the minister of energy, can make our work in Alberta much harder because we are here, as I said earlier, to protect the rights and privileges of that province.
The representatives of that province and their own legislature have drawn up programs, and I trust that the minister of energy will listen well to their presentations. Unilateral action on the part of any member of this government can destroy the confidence that we require in order to have a strong confederation. I cannot state that emphatically enough to impress upon this government the situation that can be created if they will not listen and act upon the advice that we give.
What are some of the ills that plague our confederation? What are some of the problems we have to resolve? Actually, when the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) was minister of industry, trade and commerce in the early seventies, he allowed that industry to begin to deteriorate. Under the last administration and the leadership of the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski), we in western Canada were starting to pull out of some of the problems that existed. They were mentioned in this House. 1 remember them well. The former minister of transport who is now in the other place stated that the whole transportation system was in a mess. Under the leadership and guidance of the hon. member for Vegreville, it was being brought out of that mess. 1 hope the present Minister of Transport will continue down that road of progress started by the hon. member for Vegreville.
1 must impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, that up to the present time the Minister of Transport is not off to a good start. He has created doubt in the minds of the farmers of western Canada by suggesting that he might pull out some of the support granted to the development taking place at Prince Rupert. That is not the way to engender confidence in the minds of western people, including those I represent in Alberta.
1 must also impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the members of the consortium who are also involved in this
April 16, j980

development must have the confidence of the national government that they are not going to be thwarted or misguided in their reference. Such is not the case at the present time because they are having doubts. I hope the Minister of Transport will give credence to this problem immediately and eradicate any of the doubts in the minds of those representatives who are members of the consortium.
We must never lose sight of the fact that Canada is the envy of most of the rest of the world. We are owners of the most valuable piece of real estate on this planet. We have the natural resources. We have the human resources to achieve greatness. We have the raw materials, physical and human. Do we as a people lack the knowledge and the initiative to use these resources wisely? I think not.
We have the means and the wherewithal to build a great nation but we can no longer content ourselves with temporary solutions to chronic and long-term problems. We lack an industrial strategy. What might Canada have been like today with an industrial strategy and an effective science policy? In 1978 we spent less than 1 per cent of the GNP on research and development. The United States spent 2.3 per cent; Switzerland, 2.2 per cent; West Germany, 2.1 per cent; The Netherlands, 2 per cent, Sweden, 1.8 per cent; Japan, 1.7 per cent; Scandinavia, 1.4 per cent.
In 1972 the Lamontagne science committee recommended that Canada strive for gross expenditures on research and development of 2.5 per cent of GNP by 1980. The recommendation was ignored and expenditures on research and development actually dropped below 1 per cent and have remained below 1 per cent for the past eight years.
You may wonder, Mr. Speaker, why 1 am so concerned about research and development. Let me impress upon this Parliament that the agricultural community is more dependent upon advancing research and technology than a great many businesses that we have in Canada. We require fertilizers, new types of grains, new types of equipment; what do we do with zero tillage and all that at times when energy costs are increasing?
What would the net effect have been if we had wisely planned and executed even a 1 per cent increase? What if it had been 1.94 per cent, half way between the Scandinavian countries and the 2.5 per cent recommendation of the Lamontagne committee? Economists tell us that even a 1 per cent increase starting in 1972 would have resulted in a million new jobs to date in Canada, 400,000 of them in manufacturing alone, an area where we have a tremendous debt to cope with today in the end products that are manufactured in Canada.
Wc could have created $20 billion plus in new manufacturing sales for our domestic market and for the critical export trade also. We could have created an entire new industry in the research and development field which would have generated approximately 60,000 jobs for scientists, engineers and the graduates of our universities.
Young farm people go to universities too. They cannot all find jobs on the farms. They have to go out and get jobs. We
The Address-Mr. Towers
need to have a market for our farm products. Therefore, it is all tied together and we as parliamentarians must give cognizance to that fact.
Government initiative and encouraging expenditures on research and development could have resulted in $1.5 billion in research and development expenditures by industry and a total of 2.5 billion by industry, universities and government. Industrial research and development would have been funded by the revenues of new product sales. 1 want to impress that this could have been accomplished without any cost to the taxpayer. This is what 1 like. For too long we relied on these programs being funded by the taxpayers.
Surely the time has arrived when we can expect this adequate programming to provide for its own funding. If we are to survive as a manufacturing and trading nation, we must begin with basics. We must begin with a strong research and development component in our economy. We must begin to develop the technology at home to process our own resources. Let me impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, that we in western Canada are very cognizant of this because it is what we want to do. We want to do that there because we want to keep our young people in our provinces. We must halt the process whereby we continue to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. We must accept the realization that it is not government which provides jobs in Canada but small business, manufacturing, the marketplace. Only there may be found sustaining means of improving our quality of life and safeguarding our standard of living.
Mr. Speaker, I will not take up the time of this House by dissecting the elements of the Speech from the Throne, but there are certain basic reflections 1 would leave with you. 1 am a rancher, a farmer, a small businessman, and as such 1 know I am speaking for literally thousands of people out in western Canada. Canadian small business is in trouble. Canadian small business is a victim of the cost-price squeeze. When I say "Canadian small business" I mean to include ranchers, farmers, all those involved in retailing and manufacturing. Equity is important to each and every Canadian-equity in the home, equity in the land, equity in a business. Without this equity we become serfs of government, we become crofters, tillers and workers of land we do not own because of the severe economic pressures of money and high interest rates.
increasing farm credit loans to the maximum of $100,000 is nothing more than band-aid treatment. The debt load on farmers is already too high. Extending further credit to a segment of our population already heavily committed to equity, land and equipment is tantamount to offering a drink of Kool-aid to a drowning person. High interest rates are not the answer to the basic problem. More credit is not the answer. We must look more closely at the global package of problems which confronts the farmer, the rancher, the small businessman. We must adopt measures which ensure that the small businessman is rewarded for risk venture. We must take measures to provide for the continuity of family farms.

April 16, 1980
The Address-Mr. Towers
We must cease to apply punitive tax measures which discriminate against individual initiative and the rugged work ethic. Where in the Speech from the Throne-this is an omission, I am sure-is reference made to further progress in the abolition of the capital gains tax? We must examine our capital gains law as it applies to the small businessman, the merchants, the small manufacturer, the farmer, the rancher. After all, small business is the backbone of this nation. It is the linchpin of the economy. It provides more than 70 per cent of the jobs in Canada yet it is treated as a poor cousin. Small business does not have the corporate clout, the strong voice of the multinationals. It has few champions in Parliament, it has little input into the making of the laws and regulations which affect its destiny.
Small business was dealt a particularly hard blow when the last Parliament was dissolved. Among the many progressive measures contained within the first pro-business budget in years was provision for the small business development bonds which would have resulted in lower interest rates in the smaller business community. Madam Speaker, unless the government brings back before the House some type of program of a similar nature, that is all down the drain.
Small business is being driven to the wall. If our economy is to flourish we must study and adopt economic strategies which favour all businesses in Canada, both large and small, but my emphasis today is on small business. A current publication of the Canadian Organization of Small Business, the Voice of Small Business, polled its subscribers and 75 per cent of those surveyed wanted a reduction in the size of the federal deficit. One of those who responded said: "If I consistently spend more than I earn I end up bankrupt; it is time government started operating according to the same principle as I apply to running my own business."
One of the phrases used in the Speech from the Throne causes me serious concern. We read that the government intends to increase still further the sphere of government operations. Mr. Speaker, an increase in government means increased taxes and greater burden on every Canadian. I do not think we can afford it.
Uncontrolled government spending threatens every Canadian owner-manager. Continued government deficits have led to double digit inflation which is destroying savings, eating up business investment and profits, forcing interest rates out of sight and stealing the rewards of entrepreneurial courage and hard work. We could all learn a lesson from the Dickens character who equated balanced spending with happiness and harmony and over-expenditure with misery. I hope the government is taking this to heart. Let us set ourselves to the task now.
1 want to dwell for a few moments on Bill C-28 of the last Parliament, which dealt with pensions and allowances for veterans and for their wives and families. It was interesting to observe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) introduce a motion on this subject under Standing Order 43 in the House yesterday and follow it up with a question today. Madam Speaker, it is amazing what a guilt
complex can do, even to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The NDP is well known for its support of motherhood concepts, but when members over in that corner have an opportunity to address themselves to actual legislation, they are quick to put distance between compassion and partisan politics as soon as it serves their own particular purpose. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and his colleagues had ample opportunity in the last Parliament to address themselves to a continuation of beneficial legislation. But did they? No; they placed themselves and partisan politics before the well-being of this nation. I am sure our veterans are not so naive as not to recognize grandstanding for what it is.
To sum up, this country is great and will be greater because of its people and resources. We have an awesome responsibility to develop programs and policies which pay more than lip service to this thesis. I, for one, am willing to roll up my sleeves and begin to hammer out workable solutions to longstanding problems. An old Chinese proverb declares that every journey of a thousand years requires a first step. We must take that first step to build a better Canada for all Canadians in this, the first session of the Thirty-second Parliament.

Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources): Mr. Speaker, first I would like to join all previous speakers and extend my best wishes to the distinguished members of Parliament whom we have elected to chair our meetings and our proceedings. I also want to join all those who congratulated the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. They both spoke very eloquently of their constituency and their country, and I wish them a long parliamentary career. Finally I would like to thank sincerely my electors of Outremont who gave me their confidence for the fourth consecutive time. May I simply say to them that I will try to continue to deserve the confidence they have shown in me since 1972.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment today on the diagnosis made by this government on energy conditions, our guidelines, our undertakings as well as the steps which we intend to take. I would also like to say a few words about the consequences of the PQ energy project in Quebec.

There is now a broad consensus that the world is facing a serious oil problem. We rely too much on a resource whose production and price are dictated in large part by the political whims and upheavals of an unstable Middle East. We also realize now that even if stability and reason were restored, the world would have to curb its appetite for OPEC's oil.
Strong efforts are needed for energy reasons; they are absolutely essential for economic reasons. The energy crisis is an economic crisis. Surely, everyone realizes by now that higher energy prices mean bad news for the world economy. The world is paying dearly for its failure, so far, to correct the basic imbalance between oil demand and supply. Continued failure to act will result in a worldwide economic crisis.

April 16, 1980
From a wide energy viewpoint, Canada is well off. Last year our net trade balance in energy was more than $4 billion. However, this is small comfort to Canadians worried about one commodity: oil. A country as rich in energy as Canada can and must move off OPEC oil and, as soon as possible move off the world oil market.
Canada is rich in renewable energy resources. These must play a larger role. We must also use our more plentiful natural gas and other fuels to replace oil. We must curb our demand for oil. And we will.
The energy crisis is also a crisis of Canadian nationhood. Unlike the situation in unitary states like Britain or Norway, energy benefits and burdens are not evenly shared across the country. The distinction between winners and losers is stark, easy to see, and potentially destructive. Failure to resolve this issue will jeopardize our energy future. Worse, it could pit Canadian against Canadian in a way never before witnessed in this country. Thus we must, when looking for energy solutions, first address issues of fairness and unity.
We must also address the paradox of high foreign ownership and control of the petroleum industry. There is no shortage of Canadian petroleum talent. The list of success stories grows daily. There is money available from Canadians who are among the biggest savers in the world. We must bring more Canadians into positions of ownership and control.
Mr. Speaker, there is a broad consensus on the nature of these problems. But there is no agreement on the solutions. The former Conservative government no doubt tried to respond to the problems, but they were not successful. Indeed, Parliament and the electorate rejected the approach contained in the budget because it was unfair to consumers; it would have let OPEC determine Canadian oil prices, it did not deal adequately or fairly with the revenue distribution question, it was too weak in its encouragement of substitution away from oil, and it offered little to encourage Canadian participation.
1 shall be releasing shortly an analysis of some of the budget energy proposals. For now, let me highlight some of the shortcomings 1 have noticed.
First, let us consider oil prices. The public seems to have the view that the budget package would have caused domestic prices to rise by $4 per barrel in 1980 and by $4.50 per barrel annually to 1984. The reality, however, would have been different. The budget package included continuation of payment of world oil prices to domestic oil sands plants. It also included an automatic adjustment of the domestic oil price to 75 per cent of the world price in 1983 and to 85 per cent in 1984.
The result of these factors, coupled with the dramatic increase in the world prices which, took place in 1979, is that Canadian oil prices would have risen faster than expected even at the time the pricing negotiations were under way.
If, for example, world prices were to rise from present levels at 2 per cent above the inflation rate-a very modest assumption-year-over-year changes in our price would turn out to be
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
as follows under the budget deal: In 1980, prices that consumers pay on average for petroleum products would have risen by over $7 a barrel if we include the effects of the proposed excise tax on transportation fuels; in 1981, a further $5.80; in 1982, a further $4.70; in 1983, $10.90, as the domestic price is adjusted to 75 per cent of the world price; and in 1984, $7.60 more, to reach 85 per cent of world price.
These numbers assume that we do not see a repeat of a 1979-style world price increase. Is there anyone in this House who would stake much money on that sort of optimism? No, the reality would probably have been much worse for the consumer.
Of course, no one could have predicted the world oil price outlook which we now face. No one can do so now with any confidence. And that is precisely why in today's world we would not want to link our price to OPEC's price, and that is why we want a price determined in Canada on the basis of Canadian decisions.

The budget package would also have given enormous revenues to the major producing province, Alberta. We have no quarrel whatsoever with the concept that provinces deserve a fair share of the revenues from the sale of their resources. And a fair share in Alberta's case means a province that is by far the wealthiest member, in per capita terms, of the Canadian federation.
Furthermore, we welcome the economic surge in the west. Canadians everywhere share in the excitement at what is going on there. We will do our best to help the process of sustained and diversified growth. But there must be some balance in the way the oil and gas revenues are shared. There is no preordained formula for sharing the proceeds of our energy wealth. We must seek together a fair deal.
The previous budget package, in my view, did not contain a fair deal. The budget did move to reduce the revenues which would otherwise have accrued to the industry, and we agreed with that part of the proposals. But the package offered little to help Canadian firms.
Energy is the fastest growing sector in the Canadian economy. We must transform this sector. Not only is our target 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the industry, but we want a number of the large firms to be Canadian owned and controlled and become prosperous.
The amount of the revenues currently accruing to each of the several players is important. So too, however, is the way each party will be affected by future changes in the world oil price. In our view, the budget package did not deal adequately with this.
When our economy is hit by big OPEC price hikes, federal revenues shrink and our expenditures rise as we attempt to offset the effects of the price shock. In short, the federal government loses when OPEC gains. So, too, do the governments of the energy consuming provinces. In contrast, the energy producing areas enjoy all the upside potential. I do not

April 16, 1980
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
think anyone could describe as reasonable a deal where the federal government bears the downside burden and the other parties get the upside gain.
Let me make a final comment on the budget package. We could use much more of our surplus natural gas and other commodities for our own purposes, rather than exporting more while watching oil imports grow. But our gas producing industry has an export bias. Perhaps the most important reason for this is that the profits from exports exceed by a wide margin those from domestic sales. We have a system in place which encourages producers to seek foreign markets, rather than apply their considerable talents to pushing out oil from the domestic market. We believe that was not addressed adequately in the last budget.
We believe we have a better way. Our way begins with a set of clear, strong, nationally-oriented principles. We set out these principles during the election campaign and 1 now want to confirm, in case there is any doubt, that these are the foundation for our policies and proposals.
These are our principles: security, fairness and opportunity should be the touchstones of Canadian energy policy. In oil we seek security at reasonable made-in-Canada prices. Certainly this means price levels to the consumer lower than in the budget package. We reject world prices as a standard for Canadian supply prices. We will establish a new blended oil price system incorporating the cost of domestic and imported oil. We agree without hesitation that Alberta is entitled to significantly growing per capita revenues from its oil and gas resources and that other energy-producing provinces should also benefit substantially from the sale of their resources. We want a revenue system which, without further increases in world oil prices, leaves the federal government with at least as much revenue as in the December 11 budget, without having to impose punitive taxes on the Canadian consumer.

However, the framework leaves considerable scope for movement with respect to a range of issues, as it should. We are determined to fulfil our responsibility to the country, but we will not be intransigent. Nor is there any question of our using our powers to override the legitimate rights of producing provinces. We are not declaring war on provincial powers, let alone turning the provinces into colonies or territories, as some appear to have said. On the contrary, we are determined to reach, as we have done in the past, a fair, negotiated settlement. To do so we will entertain considerable flexibility on most of the key elements of a new package: the price of old oil, the price of synthetic oil and so on. There is plenty of room to make a deal if negotiations are carried on in good faith.
1 have dwelt at some length on energy pricing and revenue sharing, but we must not become so mesmerized by these questions that we neglect other necessary actions to secure our energy furture. We will not do this. We will act to support new initiatives.
Canada faces serious economic challenges in the 1980s but it also has tremendous opportunities. It is not by a further weakening of the federal government that we will meet those challenges and those opportunities.

The debate has indeed reached a turning point. For some time now, Canadians have been witnessing the erosion of their federal administration and many are deeply shocked by it.
April 16, 1980

Mindful Canadians are well aware that a province on its own could not meet the challenges of the modern world with as much decisiveness as a large nation united in its diversity. In its most recent publication, the C. D. Howe Institute states the following:
The main selling point for federalism at this stage is that the ten provinces probably have a better chance of success in solving their economic problems if they work on them together. This conclusion is dictated primarily by the interdependence of the ten provinces occupying the Canadian economic space.
The erosion of the federal government's powers would be dangerous enough were we faced only with economic and energy problems. But we now have in Quebec a premier who wants to break up Canada and he is aiming for the logical and ultimate end product of this process, that is, total decentralization. As a Canadian, I do not feel that is proper for Canadians, and as a Quebecker I am convinced that separation, be it called independence or sovereignty-association, would be altogether disastrous for my province and for its people. Energy is an obvious example of the benefits that Quebec derives from its participation in the Canadian federation. It demonstrates also how a dynamic national energy policy makes it possible for a region to develop its own positive resources in its own way, while recognizing its responsibilities to the rest of Canada and sharing the wealth of other regions. Canadians must unite and state positively their need for a national energy policy; we have to wonder what our separatists have to offer.
Well, what do Messrs. Levesque, Pariseau and Berube, our separatists, say? They continue their long list of complaints about imaginary grievances against the rest of Canada and claim wrongly that Quebec would be better off without the rest of Canada. Quebeckers who read the papers or hear these lamentations see them immediately for the blatant nonsense they really are. There is danger, however, that this nonsense, if it is repeated often enough and not disproved, may convince those who are ill-informed. I am glad to say that several powerful voices are now being heard and contradicting the most extravagant claims of the PQ. I should like to join forces with them and mention a few examples. The PQ representatives, anxious to demonstrate their scorn for the blessings of the Canadian federation, show that they do not care much for the effects oil prices have on Quebec consumers. In fact, some PQ ministers even go so far as to say that Quebeckers should pay world prices for their oil. Are they really aware of what they are saying? If it did pay world prices, Quebec would immediately, and I insist immediately, have to pay $3.8 billion more a year for its oil, that is some $600 more for every Quebecker. And that would be only a start.
The oil pricing agreement we are seeking will be directly related to the cost of production in Canada. But Mr. Levesque and his colleagues want Quebeckers to pay the prices set by the international cartel known as OPEC. Had Quebec not been part of Canada, it would have paid, to the end of 1980, $9.5 billion more for its oil since 1974 than it will in fact.
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
thanks to the Canadian single price policy we implemented in 1974. Today, I appeal to my Quebec compatriots and beg of them, with all the conviction that I can muster, not to let themselves be taken in by those peddlers of illusions the Pequistes are. Especially in the field of energy, separatist dreams can only lead us directly to a sombre and sinister reality.
If, tomorrow morning, Quebec were to get its sovereignty-association, if, as the PQs are suggesting, it had to pay world prices for the oil it uses, as the PQ ministers would have it, every single barrel of oil in Quebec would cost $20 more than it does now, and every gallon of gas would go up by 57 cents tomorrow morning. And here is what that increase would mean in terms of the pocketbook of every Quebecker, man and woman. It would cost $400 more a year for a Quebec family to heat the home whether it be with gas or oil. A family with a car that drives about 12,000 miles a year would have to pay $450 more for gas. The taxi driver who drives some 60,000 miles a year would have to dig out of his pockets about $2,250 more to drive his cab. And the owner of a dairy farm, who uses about 2,200 gallons of diesel fuel and gas would have to pay $1,250 more a year. In addition to that, the average Quebec family would have to pay an extra $400 for non-energy product consumption, that is for all it buys that is not energy proper but which contains oil products and whose prices would naturally go up. As all those statistics are interrelated, there is nearly no limit to the additions that can be made. If you take an average Quebec family which owns a home, has a car and uses oil or gas to heat itself, well, under the PQ plan that average family tomorrow morning would pay in additional expenses an amount of $1,250 a year. That is what they are trying to sell us. That is the sad reality of the PQ ideology and that is what I am warning all Quebeckers against. The alternative is simple, progress further with Canada or move back with the PQ plan.
The Parti Quebecois also lays strong emphasis on the hydroelectric resources of the province and even talks about them as being the miracle answer to the energy problems of an independent Quebec. Here again the PQ philosophy is closer to fiction than reality. Canadians in Quebec and elsewhere are proud of the spirit of entrepreneurship and the technical competence of those men and women who made Quebec's power resources what they are today. It is a considerable asset for the province and the country as a whole. But it is nonsense to suggest, as the Parti Quebecois does, that revenues generated by the exports of hydroelectric power could compensate for the costs of imported oil at world prices. At present, Quebec consumes $6.9 billion worth a year of imported oil. If they had to pay the world price, could the sales of electric power to the United States compensate for such an amount? Far from it. If you take 1979 as an example, total sales of Quebec power to the United States would amount to about

April 16, 1980
The Address-Mr. King
$200 million to $300 million which would leave only a small deficit of about $6.6 billion. Well, the Parti Quebecois has got us used to $500 million deficits but now they are offering us a $6.6 billion deficit.
In any case, even if it were possible to strike a certain balance between the cost of imported oil and the revenues from the sales of electricity, which is not the case, Quebec would find itself in a much worse situation than the one it is and has been in. It would be more vulnerable to higher prices for imported oil, more vulnerable to embargoes and so on than we are now. A PQ minister recently worried about the possibility that Alberta oil deliveries to Montreal might dwindle in the 1980s and that Quebec would then be exposed to oil shortages, while Ontario and the western provinces would be completely protected.
Yet, this is exactly what would happen if Quebec withdrew from Canada. However, Quebec is part of Canada and will go on being part of it. Therefore, the dark prediction of the Quebec energy minister is completely false. We shall do everything possible to reduce our dependence on imported oil. However, as long as there is a risk of a shortage, this risk will be shared equally by all Canadians. This is the basis of our country. This is the profound meaning of being part of Canada. When we imagine what would be the energy and economic situation of a sovereign Quebec, we become rapidly convinced of the need to vote no to the question now asked by the Parti Quebecois.
Mr. Speaker, to remain united in spite of our differences, and united for the welfare of everyone is the only logical solution offered to all Canadians if we want to be able to face the numerous problems that will arise in the next ten years. When we speak about oil, natural gas and coal, we are speaking about sources of energy which are essential for our standard of living and quality of life, but at the same time, we are speaking about types of energy which cannot be renewed once they have been used. Not so much for ourselves as for those who will come after us, we may have to think about expanding our horizons. No province and no government alone can develop a true national energy policy. And in this area as in so many others, unity and co-operation are essential.
Mr. Speaker, we are determined to develop a true Canadian energy policy which will take into account the legitimate aspirations of the provinces and the needs of the entire country. In conclusion, I can only invite the people of Quebec not to cut themselves off and not to reduce the importance of Quebec by withdrawing from Canada at such a critical period, and not to deprive themselves of all that the rest of Canada is able and willing to provide them.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I count on you to convey to Madam Speaker on behalf of
myself and the fine Canadians whom I am honoured to represent in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen the following message:
Madam Speaker, please accept sincere, warm and appreciative congratulations on your elevation to your present exalted position. May we fortify that congratulatory message with our personal invitation to become acquainted with both the peoples and the scenic values of our favoured part of Canada by favouring us with an early visit?
I feel distinctly honoured, Mr. Speaker, to participate in the throne speech debate as the member of Parliament representing the citizens of Okanagan-Similkameen in British Columbia. Although I was a member of the Thirty-first Parliament, this marks the first occasion on which I have risen to address the House. I would therefore ask your indulgence as I briefly speak of the unique character and personality of this section of Canada which I am honoured to represent.
The riding of Okanagan-Similkameen occupies some 200 miles of international border with the United States. Its western boundary is about 150 miles from the Pacific ocean, and its eastern extremity about 200 miles from the Rocky Mountains. Its geography extends from Princeton and Merritt in the west to Grand Forks and Christina Lake in the east. It centres on the Okanagan Valley, including Osoyoos on the forty-ninth parallel to 100 miles north past the growing community of Westbank. The major city in the riding is Penticton, the city of peaches and beaches and which is also noted as the home town of the famous Penticton Vees Hockey Team, the last amateur Canadian team to capture world hockey supremacy when they defeated the Soviet Union team by the score of five to zero in the crucial final game. I was honoured to be present in Germany on that occasion.
The Okanagan Valley and its parallel counterpart, the Similkameen Valley, are world famous producers of tree fruits-apples, pears, peaches, apricots and cherries. I hope that in season I will be able to share with some of you underprivileged members of this House the incomparable flavour experience of eating freshly picked cherries from my own orchard.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In addition to orchards, these valleys now support Canada's finest vineyards. A thriving and growing wine industry has earned recognition as vintners without equal in Canada or the world. The riding contains the largest cattle ranch as well as many dozens of smaller ranches. Lumber and mining are very important elements of the economy.
Many in this chamber have visited the Okanagan and Similkameen as tourists in the summer seeking sun, sand and water which we have in abundance and in the winter for skiing at any of the dozen excellent ski facilities. Now we see the latest phenomenon of our Canadian society, attracted by its benevolent climate, its lakes and mountains, its quality of life; retired persons from across Canada are moving in increasing numbers to spend their senior years in the most ideal surroundings to be found in Canada and perhaps the world.
April 16, 1980

With that as a preamble from a native son of the Okanagan,
I will move from the virtues of my riding to an equally sincere and objective, but not so flattering, review of the government's intent as revealed in the content of the Speech from the Throne.
My riding was newly created for the May 22 election. The area has previously been represented by the CCF, the Liberals, the Social Credit and the Conservatives. 1 know that I state the obvious when I say that 1 was elected because more of the electorate endorsed my positions and policies as well as those of the Progressive Conservative Party than supported the views of the other four candidates. While this is obvious, 1 mention it because I believe we must impress on hon. members opposite that their situation in western Canada is a direct result of the rejection of the policies and the philosophical positions of their party and their leader.
Unfortunately, nothing in the Speech from the Throne would lead us to any degree of optimism that the offensive nature of that government's position has been noted in more than a cursory fashion and dismissed with the casual statement that in the west many believe their problems are ignored, their voices unheard, and their contribution is unrecognized. We believe it sincerely. There are many other descriptive phrases that could be added to the recitation of the factors that offend western Canadians. I suggest that, using the throne speech as the criterion for change, western Canadians can only look to the future with added apprehension.
Now, Mr. Speaker, permit me to respond directly to the throne speech. The Ottawa Citizen of April 15 gave it the headline, "An Admission of Errors". It went on to say:
With a fanfare of generalities, the Trudeau government has unveiled a throne speech that reads like an agenda for what it should have done during its previous I 1 years in power.
Changed circumstances, including a weak dollar, enormous government deficits and devastating interest rates (resulting largely from the cumulative effects of the spending of the past), have extracted from the government an expression of concern-
The throne speech makes no mention of a budget, no mention of a strategy designed to create an economy in which interest rates would not be set to remain competitive with U.S. rates.
It is interesting to note that in the throne speech the government chose to acknowledge duly elected members from the three western provinces under Part V of the speech, a section which is entitled "An Active Foreign Policy". I trust that the government which authored the Speech from the Throne will by its words and actions prove that that inclusion was inadvertent.
Western Canada is not foreign territory. Many of us on this side of the House ask that the government remember and recognize that fact. We are representatives of that great part of Canada, and we will resent any action which demonstrates a lack of respect for the electoral decisions taken in this past election.
Let me dispute a statement made early in the Speech from the Throne which reads;
We observe today not only the beginning of a new Parliament but the start of a new era.
The Address-Mr. King
Yes, we do have a new Parliament and we have a new decade, but we have an era complete with the same old, tired faces in the government, the same old cliches, divisive tactics, tired responses and the same old answers to the same old questions-questions raised because of the same old and damaging Liberal policies which have brought our nation to this low point in its history.
I read that "Canadians expect much of this Parliament" and I ask you if this is so, Mr. Speaker. I would doubt that such high expectation exists. Many Canadians have become cynical and embittered by the disappointments of the last dozen years. The electoral results must emphasize to hon. members opposite that the target of that cynicism in our part of Canada is Liberal policies, past and present. The question that must be addressed to hon. members opposite, Mr. Speaker, is: "Do you care?".
We read in the throne speech that "the first task is to clear the accumulation of essential legislation left from previous Parliaments". And later in the same paragraph we read:
To that end, my government is relying on the good will of members and senators of all parties.
I think I can assure hon. members of the government that they can rely on at least the same degree of co-operation and evidence of good will on the part of the opposition as they displayed in the Thirty-first Parliament in their role as the opposition. I know, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members of the government will take great comfort in my words as they review their conduct, particularly as recorded in Hansard on November 6 and 7 last year, and on most other occasions as well.
We have a legacy of national misdirection, foisted on Canada by repeated offerings of succulent expediency over a nourishing diet of basic sound policy by federal Liberal governments under disastrous leadership in the past 12 years. This legacy of Liberal government policies has led this nation to a situation which can only be described as a litany of despair and disaster-inflation, high interest, unemployment, bankruptcy and division. Where is this vaunted Liberal ability to govern? It is not to be found in history and, unfortunately for Canada's immediate future, it is not to be found in the performance of this government, judging from the content of the subject matter today.
As a western Canadian I am resentful of the tone and implications of many of the statements contained therein. Who, may 1 ask, have been the main beneficiaries of this government's past policies? The western electorate? The western electorate in the last two trips to the polls has demonstrated with some knowledge its view of confederation in action under the auspices of the Liberal government.
The sinister, underlying message contained in the throne speech is that this government is determined to centralize more power in Ottawa, to resist regional initiatives and rights, to act highhandedly with individuals and regions in the so-called name of Canada's total well-being, but with the underlying intent of changing forever the face and nature of our nation.

April 16, 1980
The Address-Mr. King
These changes are not being allowed to evolve from the concerns and aspirations of the persons who are citizens of Canada; these changes to our structures, our standards, our social order do not result from a groundswell of sentiment or persuasion but from the dictates of those opposite who seek to force philosophical, ideological and economic change insidiously upon us.
There are many vital factors that this throne speech fails to address. There is the same old theme dominating the message. We have heard it all before-the land is strong, inflation wrestled to the ground, security, equity, opportunity, the future is bright, responsible government, sharing, strengthened national institutions, economic challenges. Mr. Speaker, this government continues to be long on rhetoric and short on substance on matters of concern to Canadians.
The throne speech includes the warning that "in every part of Canada there are forces which are driving us apart rather than bringing us together". It also tells us:
To all these forces of discontent, my government has one clear response.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this response is: "Give us more power; trust us, the government that brought you such goodies as 20 per cent interest, metrification, undisciplined spending, damaging inflation, a weakened defence posture, regional, cultural and linguistic division-trust us." Trust us indeed!
We are told that "Canadians are a sensible people. They understand that these are difficult economic times throughout the world". Mr. Speaker, Canadians also understand that the difficult economic times they face as a nation are a direct result of past undisciplined action on the part of tired, uninspired government presently led by the honourable reconstituted Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
That understanding is held no more acutely anywhere than it is held in western Canada. One has only to peruse the voting pattern in the last two elections to underline that western Canadians are sensitive to what Liberal philosophical positions hold for our part of the nation.
The throne speech also tells us that "Canadians will accept sacrifice to meet the economic challenges of the 1980s, but that they will not accept injustice". Mr. Speaker, 1 trust that this government will note well, capitalize that fully and underline it distinctly. A distressed and sometimes disillusioned western Canada will not-and I repeat, will not-accept unjust confiscation of its rights and its resources.
In the next paragraph the speech tells us that "Canadians recognize the need to live within their national means". Mr. Speaker, Canadians as individuals indeed recognize this fact. Our difficulties as a nation have arisen because the government opposite has abused and reabused this basic principle and once again gives every indication that the depth of its commitment to fiscal responsibility is to indulge in cliches while its actions belie its words. The Speech from the Throne is full of promises to expand government activity, to increase control of the economy in a marked and ominous shift to the left.
The speech then states:
In particular, my government recognizes the need to protect those Canadians most affected by unacceptably high interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) includes some 10,000 Canadian mortgage holders only in that category; the other 500,000 are apparently deemed by the hon. minister to be enjoying the experience of increased mortgage payments.
"Energy policy is as important for Canada in the 1980s as railway policy was in the 1880s". The railway era was one which had as its major thrust private initiative with the supporting activities of government. We see in this throne speech a deliberate but not surprising direction taken in energy policy by a government whose disastrous record in this field speaks for itself. We see an energy policy that promises greater intervention by government. We see another government agency, the Petroleum Price Auditing Agency, set up to be the window on the agency the Liberals set up to be a window on the industry. PetroCan, which was set up by that government across the floor to be a window on the industry, will now have another agency looking into its window.
How long will this proliferation and duplication of effort by agencies of government go on? Just so long as there is a Liberal government whose objectives are self-perpetuation, larger bureaucracies, greater burdens on the taxpayer, a resolute intent to avoid realities which would require some evidence of a discipline that does not have any place in the philosophies of modern Trudeau Liberalism.
So the energy policy speaks only of greater government activity, new agencies, new measures and new directions. But surprisingly, and totally out of character with the challenging nature of the preamble which was a challenge to Canadians to seize the opportunity, there is no vision for Canada of self-sufficiency in energy matters; no such future. This government speaks instead of negotiating foreign contracts, creating greater dependence on others, which is a step away from national energy freedom. Then the government compares it to the 1880 railway era. That is irresponsible.
In the Speech from the Throne this sentence appears:
My ministers believe that Canadians want more effective government, not necessarily less government.
The Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, clearly signals that Canadians will now suffer bigger government, more government intervention in their lives, new agencies proliferating and the activities of old agencies intensified. It will be a confirmation, as Geoffrey Stevens put it, of the darkest suspicions about the socialistic predilection of the Prime Minister and his cohorts.
Canadians do want effective government. That same Liberal government under the present Prime Minister has been effective. It has effectively split our nation on regional and cultural lines. It has effectively given our nation a gross national debt whose burden voids our ability to act independently on such important basics as internal interest rates. This retreaded
April 16, 1980

Liberal government has been effective in making this energy-rich land of Canada increasingly dependent on foreign sources of petroleum products. This government has effectively and unnecessarily, by studied inattention and inaction, made our nation's industries and transportation services vulnerable to interruptions in foreign oil supply.
1 can go on and on with a recitation of this government's previous failures, but this is the effective nature of the government opposite.
I would characterize the citizens of Okanagan-Similkameen as not too different from the mainstream of citizens across Canada. They are hard-working, honest, patriotic, independent and God-fearing. They resent indifference, and particularly they resent indifference spiced with arrogance, the hallmark of Liberalism.
Please understand this: We do not ask that confederation extend us some advantage denied others. We do ask, and we insist, that we not be taken advantage of because of our loyalty to that confederation. The Prime Minister in equating happiness with prosperity does a disservice to Canadians who believe that there are other distinctive elements in the recipe. Recognition and respect are two which should notably be added, for material prosperity without the psychology of contentment means but little in the well-being of the individual, the region or the nation.
If the policy of government is addressed to favour those regions of Canada with electoral strength to the disadvantage of those areas which do not represent equivalent electoral clout, we can expect the voice for regional autonomy to become more strident.
1 have found, Mr. Speaker, that the preoccupation of the people in Okanagan-Similkameen is with national and international affairs. We are deeply concerned with the aloof stance taken by this Liberal government in its past incarnation, a stance which denied a responsible shouldering of the load to defend our freedoms against the growing threat of Soviet expansion and aggression.
Thus I am happy to note for the first time in 12 years of Liberal throne speeches a reference to our commitment to NATO. It is unseemly that it took a demonstration of Soviet aggressive intent in Afghanistan to move this government, and I await with some misgivings based on past attitudes the actions of this government backing up its throne speech statement.
Environmental concerns in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen require senior government financial assistance. Water quality considerations have the utmost priority. Limited precipitation of only 11 inches per year provides very little natural flushing action in our lakes. It takes 60 years of runoff to displace the water in Okanagan Lake. Increasing populations require immediate action. Sewage outfalls must be removed from limited flow waterways. We will be seeking means from this government to help local jurisdictions accomplish this goal.
The Address-Mr. McRae
In the throne speech reference is made to the multicultural mosaic of Canada. 1 expect recognition from this government of the aspirations of the many new Canadians in my riding to preserve certain aspects of their culture while engrossing themselves in their responsibilities as Canadians. 1 look for responsive encouragement from this government to those aspirations.
1 see nothing of substance in the throne speech for the fruit farmer or the rancher who has an operating loan of $25,000, $50,000 or $100,000 bearing interest at 20 per cent. 1 see nothing substantial to help the small independent logger struggling to make payments on his $75,000 worth of trucking equipment. I see nothing substantial to offer relief for the merchant who finds the burden of carrying stock on his shelves and on his racks beyond his capacity under the high interest rates imposed by this government's management.
1 see nothing of substance offered to young Canadians seeking to own homes. The policies which we advanced provided mortgage interest deductibility and offered operators of small businesses substantial relief from the burden of interest.
By inference, the Liberal opposition implied that they had something better to offer. The throne speech reveals the shallowness of their criticisms, the audacity of their endeavour and their overwhelming compulsion for power overcoming responsibility and reason.
